html:
A carved siltstone slab about 64 centimetres tall, made around 3100 BCE and dug up at Hierakonpolis in Upper Egypt in 1897 to 1898. It shows King Narmer and is often read as a record of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

On one side Narmer wears the white crown of the south and raises a mace over a kneeling enemy. On the other he wears the red crown of the north and inspects rows of beheaded foes. Two beasts with long, intertwined necks frame a round hollow, where an ordinary palette would hold cosmetics for grinding. His name is written in early hieroglyphs.

Scholars debate whether it shows real events or royal ideals. Either way, the pose of the king smiting his enemies became a stock image of pharaohs for three thousand years, down to the temple walls of Ramesses II. Narmer stands at the start of Early Dynastic Egypt. The palette is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
